summary: The talk opens with Awais live "vibe coding" an AI agent on chai.new by typing "chat with PDF." While it builds, he introduces his thesis: every widely used production agent—Perplexity, Cursor, v0, lovable, bolt, chai—is built on AI primitives, not frameworks. Frameworks are bloated, move too slowly relative to weekly LLM/API churn (e.g., MCP), and pile on abstractions nobody needs. Primitives, exemplified by Amazon S3, are simple low-level services that scale massively and compose freely. Awais frames AI agents as a new way of writing code and positions Langbase's goal as the fastest path to production-ready, serverless AI agents via composable primitives (memory with vector store, parser, chunker, threads, tools). The live demo creates a memory primitive, uploads PDFs that are parsed, chunked, and embedded automatically, then queries the agent correctly across files. He then enumerates eight agent architectures. First, the augmented LLM: an LLM plus auto-calling tools, threads for context, and long-term vector-backed memory. Second, prompt chaining and composition: multiple agents whose outputs gate continuation (e.g., spam classification then draft-email generation), shown with summary, features, and marketing-copy agents. Third, agent router: an LLM router that decides which specialized agent to call next—demonstrated with a summary agent (Gemini), reasoning agent (DeepSeek Llama 70B), and coding agent (Claude), routing a question about winter days to the reasoning agent. Fourth, parallel agents: multiple agents run concurrently via Promise.all with no abstraction needed. Fifth, orchestrator-worker: an orchestrator agent plans subtasks, worker agents complete them, and a synthesis agent combines results—demonstrated by generating a blog post on remote work across five subtasks in roughly 90 lines of code. Sixth, evaluator-optimizer: a generator agent produces output and an LLM-as-judge evaluator accepts or rejects with feedback, shown with an eco-friendly water bottle description refined over two iterations. Seventh, memory: upload data, create a memory, retrieve and ask questions—recapping the chat-with-PDF demo. Eighth, tool calling, briefly mentioned. Awais claims these patterns cover about 80% of complicated AI agents. He then demos a Perplexity-like deep researcher using Exa, a receipt checker using Mistral OCR plus GPT-4.1, and an image-chat agent using GPT-4o vision. He closes urging engineers to build on primitives rather than frameworks, noting new agents are built on chai.new every minute, and invites feedback on Twitter.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Intro and live vibe-coding kickoff
sections.summary: Awais opens by live vibe-coding an AI agent on chai.new with the prompt "chat with PDF," stating it will be built on AI primitives rather than a framework.

sections.title: Speaker background and frameworks-vs-primitives thesis
sections.summary: He introduces himself (contributor to WordPress, NextJS, NodeJS, React; NASA helicopter mission; former VP roles) and asserts that production agents from Perplexity, Cursor, v0, lovable, bolt, and chai are not built on frameworks, which are bloated and slow; instead they use primitives, likened to Amazon S3.

sections.title: LLM journey and agents as a new way to write code
sections.summary: Awais recounts receiving GPT-3 access from Greg Brockman in 2020 and building Copilot-like tooling a year before GitHub Copilot launched; he frames AI agents as a new way of writing code too consequential to encase in a framework, suggesting small composable blocks like threads.

sections.title: Langbase mission and primitive vision
sections.summary: As most engineers transition toward AI engineering, Langbase aims to be the fastest path to production-ready serverless AI agents via composable cloud primitives (memory with vector store, parser, chunker, threads, tools).

sections.title: Live demo: chat with PDF
sections.summary: chai.new auto-creates a memory and an agent; Awais uploads PDFs (about page, talks page, Langbase API-key doc) that are parsed, chunked, and embedded, then queries the agent about the founder's last three talks and how to get an API key, receiving correct cross-file answers; a bug is noted as fixable in app mode.

sections.title: Behind the scenes: primitives and stateofaiagents.com
sections.summary: He explains the underlying primitives—memory as an autonomous drag/workflow engine, threads for context, parser, chunker—and references research at stateofaiagents.com on how agents are built across industries.

sections.title: Architecture 1: Augmented LLM
sections.summary: The first architecture is an augmented LLM: an LLM with auto-calling tools (MCPs/APIs), threads for conversation context and scratch-pad state, and long-term vector-backed memory that can hold terabytes; together these primitives can build almost any agent.

sections.title: Architecture 2: Prompt chaining and composition
sections.summary: Prompt chaining uses multiple agents whose outputs gate continuation—e.g., classify an email as spam before drafting a response. Demonstrated with summary, features, and marketing-copy agents working together in plain JavaScript/TypeScript.

sections.title: Architecture 3: Agent router
sections.summary: An LLM router agent decides which specialized agent to call next. Demo uses three agents—summary (Gemini), reasoning (DeepSeek Llama 70B), coding (Claude)—and routes a question about why days are shorter in winter to the reasoning agent, which produces the answer. All built with primitives, no framework.

sections.title: Architecture 4: Parallel agents
sections.summary: Multiple agents run concurrently using JavaScript Promise.all—e.g., sentiment, summary, and decision-maker agents. No abstraction layer is needed; it is plain old code.

sections.title: Architecture 5: Orchestrator-worker
sections.summary: An orchestrator agent plans and creates subtasks for worker agents, whose outputs are synthesized. Demoed with a blog post on remote work benefits, split into five subtasks (intro, productivity, work-life balance, environmental impact, conclusion), each handled by a worker agent, then synthesized. Roughly 90 lines of code, no framework. Awais warns that framework abstractions will make migration hard as LLMs improve at agentic workflows.

sections.title: Architecture 6: Evaluator-optimizer
sections.summary: A generator agent produces output (e.g., marketing copy for an eco-friendly water bottle) and an LLM-as-judge evaluator accepts or rejects it with feedback. First iteration rejected for missing the eco-conscious millennial audience; second iteration accepted after specific feedback. Awais recommends using the best available LLM for evaluation.

sections.title: Architecture 7: Memory and architecture 8: Tool calling
sections.summary: The memory pattern uploads data, creates a memory primitive, retrieves relevant context, and an agent answers questions—recapping the chat-with-PDF demo. Tool calling is briefly mentioned but skipped. Awais states these eight patterns cover about 80% of complicated AI agents.

sections.title: Demo agents: deep researcher, receipt checker, image chat
sections.summary: Awais demos a Perplexity-like deep researcher using Exa for web search, asked about latest OpenAI news; a receipt checker using Mistral OCR plus GPT-4.1 that correctly extracts City of Palo Alto and $15 from a parking ticket image; and an image-chat agent using GPT-4o vision that analyzes a facial expression from an image URL.

sections.title: Closing remarks
sections.summary: Awais notes new agents are built on chai.new almost every minute—dental cost advisor, business swap pro, task refiner, etc.—all on AI primitives, not frameworks. He reiterates that frameworks add little value in a fast-moving space with weekly new paradigms and LLMs, urges engineers to build on primitives or use pre-built ones from Langbase and others, invites feedback on Twitter, and signs off.
